topic: bringing a derelict overshot watermill back into work: leat, wheel bearings and dressing the stones

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: licznik obrotow na wale glownym

base: I am putting an old overshot watermill back to work after thirty years standing idle.
A sawmill downstream still runs an undershot wheel off the very same leat.
I fitted a revolution counter to the main shaft, because guessing the speed proved hopeless.
Several buckets on the wheel have rotted away and the rim is badly worn.
Should I rebuild the wheel first, or clear the leat and see what water arrives?
Clear the leat first, because the wheel you build depends entirely on the water you have.
Thirty years of silt will have halved the flow reaching your launder.
Measure the head and the flow before you cut a single new bucket.
A wheel built for water that never comes will disappoint you for years.
I cleared the leat over three weekends and the flow has more than doubled.
The revolution counter shows nine turns a minute with the sluice fully open.
The wheel groans badly on the upstroke and the shaft seems to lift slightly.
Is that the bearings, or has the whole wheel gone out of true?
That is the bearings, since a shaft that lifts is riding on worn brasses underneath.
Nine turns a minute is right for an overshot wheel of that diameter.
Lift the shaft, scrape the brasses to a true bearing and pack them again.
A groaning wheel wears its own gudgeons away within a single working season.
I scraped and repacked both brasses and the groaning has gone completely away.
The revolution counter now holds steady at nine turns even under load.
That sawmill wheel downstream runs much faster, though its stream looks no larger.
Why should an undershot wheel turn quicker on apparently the same water?
An undershot wheel takes its power from speed, while yours takes power from weight.
Water falling into your buckets does its work by simply being heavy there.
A fast wheel needs a fast stream and gives far less power for it.
Your nine turns will drive a pair of stones better than his thirty ever could.
I coupled the stones up and ran them empty for about an hour yesterday.
The runner stone rides evenly but the meal comes out coarse and uneven.
The furrows look shallow and the lands are polished almost smooth in places.
Do I dress the stones now, or try adjusting the tentering first?
Dress the stones, because no amount of tentering will cure a polished, worn-out land.
The furrows do the cutting and the lands do the final grinding.
Once both are worn flat the meal comes through in coarse, ragged flakes.
Deepen the furrows with a mill bill and crack the lands lightly all over.
I dressed both stones with a mill bill over the best part of a week.
The meal now comes through fine and cool, exactly as the old miller described.
My arms have never ached so much in the whole of my life.
How often must a working pair of stones be dressed like this?
Every three weeks of steady work, though soft wheat will let you go longer.
Watch the meal rather than the calendar, since the flour tells you first.
Warm meal at the spout always means the lands have begun to rub.
Keep the bill sharp and the dressing itself grows lighter every time.
